question: How long can a traveller keep shortening prayers once staying at a temporary destination?
answer:
Okay, the next question, which is the long one now: how long can you do qasr for? How long can you do qasr for? This is the big issue of today. So we divide this question — this is question number five I'm doing today — into two scenarios, 5A and 5B.

Well, before we even get to 5A and 5B: what is the scenario we're talking about? We're talking about you have arrived at a temporary destination. We are not talking about en route. No scholar says that there's a limit en route. People would take two and a half months or three months to go from Morocco to Mecca — three months — and the whole route is obviously qasr, because you're a musafir. You're walking, riding a camel. There is no question about the time frame of the safar itself.

And subhanAllah, by the way, these days it takes us less than 17 hours — 15 hours, direct flight, Dallas to Australia, and I've done that flight as well, subhanAllah, a direct flight. And subhanAllah, it took them three months to do a four-hour, five-hour flight, and — Allah's blessings on us — we just do the whole world and we come back. SubhanAllah, Allah's blessings on us.

So the point being that nobody is questioning the length of the safar; however long it is, you will do qasr. Now you get to your temporary destination. This is not your house. You are sent by your company to a city for training; you're visiting friends; you're attending a shaadi, a wedding, somewhere. You're staying for X number of days. You are now in a hotel or in somebody's house; you are no longer on the road. This is the scenario. Okay, you understood?

Now, this scenario is divided into two, 5A and 5B. Scenario A: you genuinely do not know when you will be returning, and every day presents the potential of you returning. Now, this is difficult for us to imagine, because we book our flights. Let me give you — in the good old days you had multiple such issues. Of them: you're engaged in an actual war and you're sent to the front of the line, and every day you don't know. You might be moving somewhere, you might be staying, you might be attacking, you might be withdrawing. Every day is a state of uncertainty.

Another example, which may be realistic: suppose you're driving, and it is wintertime, and you're in a cold place, and the roads are shut down because of snow. And you want to leave, but you don't know when the roads will open. Maybe tomorrow, maybe three days, maybe five days; you don't know. So you wake up every day wanting the road to be open, but you don't know how long.

So if you are in a state of uncertainty, in this case your ruling is the ruling of the actual musafir, because you want to leave, or you don't know when you will leave. And it is authentically reported that Ibn Umar and others were in Azerbaijan, and they did qasr for more than six months. Some say some Sahaba did qasr for two years in the battlefield. Battlefield means they were on the front lines, moving here, moving there. They're obviously not fighting every day, but they are in the state of the battlefield: every day, tactical maneuver, this and that. They're praying qasr for two years because they're not setting up house. They're not building an apartment complex and getting married and having kids. This is an obvious state of flux. So if you do not know when you will return, then you will remain in qasr, because it is uncertain. You could return today, you could return tomorrow, a week; you don't know.

Now, that scenario is, I think, rare for most of us. The other scenario is going to be the big controversial issue: what if you have a good idea? I'm staying here five days, that's my intention. You intend to stay seven days, one week. Your company sends you for an assignment, and it is a three-month-long assignment. You know it is three months, and after three months, that's it, you're going to come back home. Or you're sent for training, six weeks training, and you know it's training, so you know exactly how long it is going to be.

So this issue is the one that, just like last week, there are lots of opinions. In fact, some 'ulama have listed 20 opinions on this issue, 20 different opinions. Some have said the duration is 20 days long. Ibn Abbas and Ishaq ibn Rahwayh said 19 days long. The hadith is in Bukhari, that Ibn Abbas said: once I prayed with the Prophet ﷺ 19 days doing qasr. This was in Tabuk. So if I'm traveling for 19 days, I'll do qasr, and if I'm traveling for more than that, I won't do qasr. Who said this? Ibn Abbas, not the Prophet ﷺ. He's deriving from Tabuk, that he stayed there 19 days doing qasr: so that's my limit that I have derived.

Other scholars said 17. Others said 13. Al-Awza'i said 12. Ali ibn Abi Talib said 10 days. Hasan al-Basri said three days. Rabi'at al-Ra'y said one day: if you're going to stay one day, you stop praying qasr. And so in early Islam we had over 20 opinions about this, how long.

Once again, all of them are trying to derive from the life of the Prophet ﷺ a number. Our Prophet ﷺ did not explicitly state, you may continue to do qasr for this many days and then you must swap over. In the famous books of hadith there is nothing like this whatsoever. What do we have? Derivations. Like we explicitly found Anas deriving. Anas said: I accompanied the Prophet ﷺ for 19 days and we did qasr. So I have derived from this: if I travel for 19, I'll do qasr, and if it's more than 19, I won't do qasr. So he is getting it from the qasr of the Prophet ﷺ for 19 days.

Now, obviously, once upon a time fiqh was much more vibrant, and 'ulama were giving their positions. And then we have the era of the flourishing of the madhhabs, and then we have the era of codification and ossification. So what happens is, out of all of these 20 opinions, essentially only two make their way into the madhhabs. Because again, fiqh had different stages, and the madhhabs basically evolved and codified, and made things in many ways easy as well, and in many ways, as we said, they kind of had their position.

So essentially what happened is we have two major camps. The first camp is the Hanbali, the Shafi'i and the Maliki school, and essentially all of these say that qasr is only done for three days: if you know you're going to spend more than three days, then no qasr. Now, I said generally. Technically the Hanbalis say 20 salah, so they count by salah; they will literally count by salah. Whereas the Shafi'is say you ignore the day of arrival. So basically there's the issue of 20 salah for the Hanbalis, and then the Malikis and Shafi'is say that once you go to the fourth day, then you become a muqim. Once you get to the fourth day, then you are no longer able to do safar.

And what is their main evidence? And again, all of these are derived. We have evidences, but they're derived; they're extracted from things of the Prophet ﷺ. The Hanbalis bring forth the hadith in Sahih Muslim that the Prophet ﷺ arrived in Mecca to perform Hajj on the morning of the 4th of Dhul Hijjah, and he prayed Fajr in Mecca, and he prayed all of the 4th, and all of the 5th and 6th and 7th, all of them in qasr, and that was 20 salawat. Then he prayed Fajr outside of Mecca, in the valley of Abtah, and qasr began from there, in Mina. So they derived 20 salah from the 4th, 5th, 6th and 7th of Dhul Hijjah. Do the numbers: 5, 10, 15, 20 salawat.

The other three madhhabs, they said — I made a mistake, clearly. It was not three days, it was four days. I made a mistake: beyond the fourth day I wanted to say, not beyond the third day. Beyond the fourth day. So the other three madhhabs also derive the fourth day: if you are traveling for four days, the final of the fourth day, you will not do qasr. However, the way that they calculated it, they said you don't look at the day you arrive; you look at the evenings. So the Shafi'is might allow 22 salah, let's say, but definitely not 25 salah. So the Shafi'is and the Malikis are a little bit different in how they define, but essentially the time frame is 20 salawat for the Hanbalis and four days for the others. Not three days — that was a slip of the tongue — four days.

Now, this is the other madhhabs. Another evidence that they use — they have a number of derivations — is that the Prophet ﷺ told the Muhajirin to not stay longer than three days in Mecca. But again, the response is that that was about the muhajir. They were prohibited from returning to Mecca permanently: once you've done hijrah to Medina, you're not allowed to reside in Mecca. And their point is, okay, this is residing; the prohibition is there. So once again they derive it from there. So this is the three madhhabs.

The Hanafis are the only madhhab that took another position, and that is 15 days. 15 days. And they don't have any explicit evidence for 15, but they make qiyas upon various things which are not directly related. For example: what is the maximum number of tuhr days of the lady of hayd? It's not exactly related to salah, but they somehow derive from this that you can stay 15 days. And so on the 16th day — if you're going to stay 16 days or more — then you are not allowed to do qasr; you must perform the full salah.

Now obviously, you heard me last week, and we went over that the distances are all derived. Well, now you've seen yourself that the numbers that people are taking are also extracted. Nothing explicit. So whoever wishes to follow their madhhab, alhamdulillah, that is good. And as you know my position: I encourage the following of the madhhabs, generally speaking, but I am not a fanatical follower. I don't think it is healthy for every single issue, especially those that deal with modern issues of living in the modern world, and this we leave to our modern scholars to talk about. Sometimes we need to rethink through. So in this issue, if you wish to follow your madhhab, I have told you what it is: for three of the madhhabs it is 20 rak'ah or four days, and for the Hanafis it is 15 days.

As usual, Ibn Taymiyyah comes along and he rocks the boat. And it's not only Ibn Taymiyyah, others as well. Ibn Taymiyyah is very clear that whoever says there is a number of days that you're going to be a musafir — either 3 or 4 or 10 or 12 or 15 — has brought forth a statement upon which there is no evidence, la dalila 'alayh. This is Ibn Taymiyyah's position: that there is no evidence from the Shari'ah.

Now, the problem with this is the implication: that you could be a musafir for a long period of time. What if your company sends you for six months? Isn't that common, that you have an assignment for six months? And so for six months, are you going to be a musafir for six months? Believe it or not, some modern followers of Ibn Taymiyyah, including our dear Shaykh and teacher, my own teacher, Shaykh Ibn Uthaymeen, Allah yarhamuh, would very clearly give this fatwa. He would follow this to its logical conclusion — even though Ibn Taymiyyah never said that, by the way; he didn't open the door for six months. But our Shaykh, may Allah bless him — and again, to quote an opinion is simply... this is not an emotional thing. I love him more than anybody can who hasn't studied with him, but it is an opinion of his, and I respectfully disagree. But he would publicly say this; I heard this with my own ears, and it's well known in his fatawa.

Students would come to him. He's of course a Saudi scholar, and Saudi students were sent to this country — I think now it's almost dwindled down — but they were sent to this country for four years at a time, five years at a time. A student comes to him and says, 'Shaykh, the government has sent me to America for four years, and I know I'm here for four years. I have no intention of remaining more than four years. May I consider myself a musafir?' And he would very publicly say, 'Yes, you are a musafir.' Now, that position is almost unprecedented and unheard of, but it is the logical conclusion if you go the full way.

Ibn Taymiyyah himself did not go that far. Ibn Taymiyyah is very clear. Somebody asked him — and I have the references here — 'I intend to stay in a city for one month, and then I plan to return.' Ibn Taymiyyah said that the better opinion for you, the safer position for you, is that you do not do qasr for one month; you pray the full for one month. This is explicit: like, this is too long. That's what he's trying to say.

This position of Ibn Taymiyyah is basically the one I'm very sympathetic to, which is: use your common sense, but don't be foolish. Like the four-day limit or the 20 rak'ah limit: what if it's 21 rak'ah? It changes? Doesn't make any sense. It's too hardcore; the demarcation is too black and white. Now, the defense of the fuqaha is: we want that demarcation to be black and white; we want it to be explicit, or else we open the door of confusion. And they're absolutely right; it does open the door for confusion if you want to. That's why Ibn Taymiyyah's fatwa was: whoever wants to stick with four days, alhamdulillah, good, that is the majority opinion. But if you are going for a reasonable amount of time...

Now, what is the position that I personally follow in my life? The way that I view my safar: **if I'm living out of a suitcase, then I'm a musafir.** At times I have been for five days to a city. Five days is more than the four-day limit, but five days for me is complete safar. However, if somebody were to go and rent an apartment, even if it's a long-term, month-by-month apartment, for example; if somebody goes and finds out where's the masjid, where's the halal food; if somebody goes and enrolls his kids in the school and says, 'I'm only here for six months,' but my kids... this is not safar anymore.

So again, it's a logical or reasonable frame of mind: are you even temporarily settling down? In my humble opinion, six months, you are settling down. You're going to have a car or means of transportation; you're going to know the restaurants, halal restaurants; you're going to make some friends; you're going to have some social life there. Whereas four or five days, you might just be in your bubble of corporate and back to the hotel, and corporate and back to the hotel. You know what that psychological frame is.

So, bottom line, Ibn Taymiyyah's position: if you want to stick to the four, it's fine. If it's a little bit more than this, okay, no big deal, as long as you're actually a musafir. So this is what I agree with, and inshallah that is the correct one.
